source.title: When Data Is Scarce: Scaling Sparse Language Models with Repeated Training
source.authors: Bo-Qian Wu; Qiao Xiao; Patrik Okanovic; Tomasz Sternal; M. van Keulen; Mykola Pechenizkiy; E. Mocanu; T. Hoefler; D. Mocanu

record.file_problem: not stated; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends language-model scaling experiments to dynamic sparse training with limited unique data and repeated training, a setting distinct from the dense scaling regimes in the original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own sparse and dense training sweeps, fitted scaling laws, and extrapolation results. Cited findings from prior scaling-law papers are not recorded as rows. Learning-rate sweep results in Appendix C are omitted because they do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains about 500 LLaMA-2 models on C4 with dynamic sparsity and repeated data. It fits Chinchilla- and Muennighoff-style power-law loss laws and checks extrapolation on held-out larger models. Its results therefore bear on V1, V2, V3, V5 and V7 in a new setting: sparse, data-constrained pretraining.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that dynamic sparsity delays repeated-data saturation (Rd* rises from 4.4 to about 6.9 at S=0.5). They propose a sparsity-aware data-constrained law that fits and extrapolates well. Sparsity shifts fixed-data allocation toward more epochs and a smaller N/D ratio. Loss-optimal sparsity is about 50%, compute-optimal sparsity rises with data scale, and it matches dense loss with about 8–10× fewer sparse FLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures dynamic sparse pretraining with repeated data and fits a sparsity-aware, data-constrained law; it is not a reproduction of the original dense scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with sparsity, model size, unique-token budget, repetition, and compute definition. The leave-one-density sensitivity analysis reports wider uncertainty near dense and extreme-sparsity boundaries than in the moderate-sparsity region.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed non-zero parameters, validation loss falls mildly with sparsity, then plateaus or rises at extreme sparsity (U-shaped). It stays monotone when N is small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under fixed unique data, loss is U-shaped in sparsity at a fixed non-zero parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted law predicts loss-optimal sparsity of about 0.45–0.5 across data budgets. Compute-optimal sparsity rises from about 0.6 to 0.7 with Ud and matches dense loss with about 8–11× fewer FLOPs. The 13B and 130B points are extrapolated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sparse data-constrained training, compute-optimal sparsity increases with the unique-data budget while loss-optimal sparsity stays moderate.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study focuses primarily on C4 and models below frontier LLM scale; the authors say domains may have different repetition dynamics. The proposed law is phenomenological, and sparse-FLOPs results are idealized relative to practical hardware efficiency. The main fit and allocation results do not report uncertainty intervals; the sensitivity analysis is specifically about curve shape.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were left out. Appendix C learning-rate sweeps were excluded because they do not measure a claim version.

untested.parts: Dense infinite-data scaling over several orders of magnitude in compute. Active N spans only about 15M–960M.
Extrapolation orders of magnitude beyond the fit range. Held-out models are only about 2–4× larger; no per-size errors are given.
An empirical IsoFLOP sweep establishing the exponents across compute. The equal split is derived from a fit with tied α and β.
Entire version: no depth or width variation at fixed N.
Comparison of published exponents and the effect of fitting method or schedule. Only a leave-one-density refit is done.

missing.what: Iso-FLOPs comparison under sparse versus dense FLOP accounting. An intermediate-sparsity optimum appears under both, but the gains depend on how compute is counted: a parameter-counting choice relevant to V7.
missing.locator: Section 4.2; Figure 5; Appendix D.1.1 dense-FLOPs derivation

missing.what: Leave-one-density refits: the compute-saving factor ranges 7.3±1.4× to 10.9±1.6×, and the curve shape is least stable near dense and extreme sparsity.

record.verdict_notes: The reported coefficients are internally inconsistent. Figure 3 and Appendix D.1 give different A, B and E. Rd* and Rn* are swapped between the main text (Rd*=4.4) and Appendix D.2 (Rd*=11.09, Rn*=4.40). The fit range is stated as 1.92B in the abstract versus 3.84B in the appendix. The α=β equality makes the Chinchilla-like 0.5 split partly a modelling outcome. No uncertainty is given for the main fits. Removed the reader's V7 label on R7, which was not linked to V7. All runs are on C4, with active models at or below 960M.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the infinite-data, non-bottleneck regime across several orders of magnitude for dense language models; most experiments concern sparse training with finite data.
No separately stated quantitative result for each held-out model size; the reported validation fit aggregates held-out configurations.

The derived compute exponents are for the fitted scaling law under sparse-FLOPs allocation without repetition. It does not establish a general compute-optimal trend across dense and repeated-data settings.
No tests of other modalities, fine-tuning or transfer; experiments use C4 and dynamic sparse pretraining with repeated data.

Does not compare competing published exponents or systematically vary fitting methods and training schedules; the reported results concern saturation under sparsity and repetition, plus a leave-one-density sensitivity analysis.

The held-out models reach 7.68B dense-equivalent, which is only 2–4× beyond the fit range, not orders of magnitude. Validation R² (0.914) is lower than fitted R² (0.982).

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 family (aggregate over dense and sparse model configurations)
rows.size_stated: 15M to 3.84B parameters in the fitting procedure
rows.operation_detail: Fit the proposed sparsity-aware loss law to validation losses on unique data.
rows.note: The fitted law includes a sparsity-dependent parameter term; the reported fit combines dense and sparse configurations.
rows.check: The law keeps a power law in non-zero N and D, with a sparsity-dependent prefactor. The fitted α and β are identical to 8 digits (0.32682177), which suggests they were tied in the fit. Coefficients in Figure 3 (A=189, B=447, E=2.35) differ from those in Appendix D.1 (A=5.24, B=6.10, E=0.85).

rows.subject: Dense LLaMA-2 models (aggregate over model configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Fit the dense repeated-data scaling law using effective data and effective parameter counts.
rows.note: The fit uses the previously fitted coefficients and estimates the repetition saturation parameters.
rows.check: The fit is in effective-data form. Removed V7: this fit row itself does not show curve bending; R6 does. The appendix gives Rd*, Rn* = [11.09, 4.40], while Figure 3 and the main text give Rd* = 4.4 and Rn* = 11.1, i.e. swapped. Size is not stated.

rows.subject: Sparse LLaMA-2 models (aggregate over model configurations)
rows.stage_stated: dynamic sparse pretraining with repeated data
rows.operation_detail: Fit sparsity-dependent data and parameter saturation terms to repeated-data results.
rows.note: The fitted law represents repeated data through effective dataset size and sparsity-dependent saturation thresholds.
rows.check: Removed V7 for the same reason as R3. This is a fit-quality row for the sparse repeated-data law.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 family (aggregate across tested active parameter sizes and data budgets)
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss as sparsity increased at fixed non-zero parameter budgets and data settings.
rows.value: Loss decreases mildly with increasing sparsity, then plateaus or slightly increases at higher sparsity; the paper says the dependence is U-shaped overall and can remain monotonically decreasing when N is sufficiently small.
rows.note: The text describes the aggregate trend across settings; exact curve values are presented graphically.
rows.check: Loss versus sparsity at fixed non-zero N measures the effect of sparsity, not a power law in N, D or C, nor fit-dependence of exponents. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 family (aggregate over tested model sizes)
rows.stage_stated: pretraining with unique or repeated data
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation-loss trajectories for repeated-data training with trajectories for an equivalent amount of unique data.
rows.measure: Validation-loss gap and saturation with additional training
rows.baseline: Training on an equivalent amount of unique data
rows.value: Repeated-data models plateau earlier; the gap grows with model size at fixed data budget and repetition ratio, and shrinks as the unique-token budget increases. Sparsity narrows the gap most noticeably around 0.5; at higher sparsity the additional narrowing is more modest.
rows.note: These are stated aggregate comparisons; Figure 2 plots individual configurations.
rows.check: Repeated-token training plateaus earlier than unique-data training, so loss in raw tokens bends away from a single power law (observed for V7). The power-law form holds for repeated data only after the effective-data saturation correction (partial for V5).

source_check.correct: V5: partial for scaling in raw presented tokens. V7: observed, because repeated-data trajectories plateau earlier and depart from unique-data scaling.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 2 and caption, lines 367–525; discussion, lines 651–688.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state understates the directly observed fit-dependence named by V7.

rows.subject: Fitted sparse data-constrained scaling law
rows.operation_detail: Minimized the fitted no-repetition loss law under a sparse-FLOPs compute constraint.
rows.value: Fitted α = 0.32682177 and β = 0.32682177; the paper derives N* ∝ C^(α/(α+β)) and D* ∝ C^(β/(α+β)), so each exponent is 0.5 for these fitted values.
rows.note: The paper states that sparsity changes constant prefactors but not these compute exponents in this fitted formulation.
rows.check: The 0.5/0.5 exponents are derived analytically from the fitted law, not measured from an IsoFLOP sweep. Because α equals β exactly, equal scaling is effectively built into the fit. This holds only under sparse-FLOPs accounting with no repetition.

source_check.correct: N* ∝ C^(β/(α+β)); D* ∝ C^(α/(α+β)). The fitted α=β=0.32682177 makes both derived exponents 0.5.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix D.1, fitted coefficients, line 1841; Appendix D.1.1, Equations 30–32, lines 1877–1912.
source_check.problem: The row assigns α/(α+β) to N*, whereas the paper assigns β/(α+β); equal fitted exponents conceal the error numerically.

rows.subject: Dense and 50%-sparse LLaMA-2 models (aggregate frontier examples)
rows.size_stated: Dense example about 2B non-zero parameters; sparse example about 1B non-zero parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared near-optimal allocations along the fixed-data compute frontier.
rows.measure: Near-optimal parameter count, epochs and parameter-to-token ratio
rows.baseline: Dense: about 8 epochs, roughly 2B non-zero parameters, N/D ≈ 0.19
rows.value: Sparse: about 12 epochs, roughly 1B non-zero parameters, N/D ≈ 0.064; approximately 3× smaller parameter-to-token ratio
rows.note: This is a comparison of sparse and dense allocations at an example compute scale, not a sweep establishing a compute-power trend.
rows.check: At fixed data, the dense data-constrained frontier departs from the Chinchilla single-epoch frontier. 50% sparsity shifts the optimum toward more epochs: N/D 0.064 versus 0.19. The compute-optimal split therefore depends on the data regime and sparsity: observed for V7, a qualification of V3's stable allocation. This is one example at about 1e20 FLOPs.

source_check.correct: V7: observed allocation dependence on sparsity at fixed unique data. V3: cannot_determine from this comparison; it does not establish whether optimal parameter and token counts follow stable powers of compute.
source_check.problem: Partial conflates an observed setup-dependent allocation shift with an unmeasured change in compute-power stability.
